summary: Mission Control is a browser game where players design, manage and simulate a complete space mission from concept to operation. Players choose one of five scenarios (Earth orbit, Moon, asteroid, Mars landing and Jupiter) and build a spacecraft by selecting a launch vehicle, bus, power system, antenna, propulsion, science instruments, shielding and landing system. A live dashboard shows how each choice affects budget, mass, Δv, power, data downlink and expected science. The mission is then simulated through launch, cruise, orbit insertion or landing, and science operations. During the simulation, random events such as solar flares, dust storms, instrument failures and budget cuts force trade-off decisions. Each run ends with a mission report and a post-mission analysis that explains why the mission succeeded or failed. The game makes abstract engineering trade-offs concrete for students and can be played solo, cooperatively or competitively.
details:
What it does

Mission Control is an interactive mission design and simulation game. It turns the competing demands of a real space mission into decisions with visible consequences. Players:

1. Pick a scenario (Earth Observation Satellite, Lunar Mapping Orbiter, Asteroid Sample Mission, Mars Surface Laboratory or Jupiter System Probe) and a difficulty (Easy, Normal or Hard).

2. Design a spacecraft by choosing a launch vehicle, bus size, solar panels, RTGs, batteries, antenna, chemical or ion propulsion, fuel, up to 8 science instruments, radiation shielding, redundancy and a landing system.

3. Watch a live dashboard (budget, mass vs. launch capacity, Δv, power, data link, estimated science) and an engineering review that flags problems. A drawing of the spacecraft updates with every part.

4. Launch and simulate the mission through launch, cruise, orbit insertion or landing, and science operations. Gauges show resources in real time.

5. Respond to 11 types of random events, such as solar flares, micrometeoroids, software errors, reaction wheel failures, fuel leaks, Mars dust storms, solar conjunction, comet opportunities, instrument failures, budget cuts and Jupiter radiation belts. Each event is a trade-off decision.

6. Get a mission report (score, chart of science and health over time, event timeline) and a post-mission analysis that explains why the mission succeeded or failed and names the biggest bottleneck.
